hub_name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Across law, accounting, medicine, research and finance, the thing a client used to pay for is becoming cheap to produce. A first draft of a contract, a categorised trial balance, a literature review or a set of comparable companies can now be generated in minutes. What does not get cheaper is deciding whether the draft is right for this client, this risk and this moment. The professional's value moves from producing the artifact to judging it: the lawyer who reads the generated contract against the client's actual goal, the accountant who advises on what the model's cash flow forecast means, the analyst who decides whether a generated valuation deserves the committee's trust.
sections.heading: The deliverable stops being the product

sections.body: PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, built on more than a billion job advertisements across 27 countries, describes a two-track market. In professionalised roles, where AI amplifies expert judgment, radiologists and recruiters among them, job growth is twice as fast and salaries rise 42 percent faster than in democratised roles, where AI makes the work easier for non-experts. Workers with AI skills now command an average wage premium of 62 percent, up from 57 percent a year earlier. The same report finds that entry-level roles exposed to AI in the United States are seven times more likely to ask for traditionally senior skills such as judgment and leadership.
sections.heading: The labour market is splitting in two

sections.body: For generations, junior lawyers, first-year accountants, residents and research assistants learned by doing the repetitive work: document review, reconciliations, first drafts, literature searches. That work is exactly what AI absorbs first. PwC's data shows the split already: AI-exposed entry roles that demand senior skills grew 35 percent since 2019, while other entry-level roles fell 10 percent. Firms can no longer rely on routine work to season their people. The juniors who remain are managing and checking machine output from their first week, which means firms have to teach judgment, client handling and the auditing of AI deliberately, rather than hoping it arrives with time served.
sections.heading: The apprenticeship is breaking

sections.body:
When an AI system drafts, diagnoses or recommends, the professional who signs still owns the result. A fabricated citation in a brief is the lawyer's problem; a symptom invented by an ambient scribe is in the physician's chart. Insurers have noticed. From January 2026, Verisk's ISO forms let carriers attach a generative AI exclusion to commercial general liability policies: CG 40 47 removes bodily injury, property damage and personal and advertising injury arising from generative AI, CG 40 48 removes the personal and advertising injury part alone, and CG 35 08 applies the exclusion to products and completed operations. The endorsements are optional, so the question for any firm is what its own endorsement schedule says, and whether its documented oversight would satisfy a carrier or a court.

The risk also runs the other way. In January 2026, Judge Jesse Furman of the Southern District of New York, who chairs the federal judiciary's Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules, told a New York State Bar Association panel that he could foresee a day when a lawyer who does not use AI is the one committing malpractice. His example was a fee dispute: a client challenging thousands of billed hours as unreasonable because an AI tool could have done the same tasks in moments. It was a remark on a panel, not a ruling, and no court has held it. But it frames the professional's position precisely: liable for what the machine gets wrong, and increasingly answerable for declining to use it at all.
sections.heading: The professional becomes the liability sink

sections.body: Generative AI produces content when asked; agentic AI takes steps. An agent notices a problem, checks options, updates a system, issues a refund or a trade within its limits, and reports back. That is where the professions feel the change most sharply, because an agent that acts inside a client's accounts, records or matters needs the controls a junior employee would: a named owner, the least access its task needs, approval gates for anything irreversible, and a record of every action. The security and governance work on this site, the six security domain pages and the Agent Development Lifecycle among them, is written for exactly this shift.
sections.heading: From generating to acting

sections.body: When any firm can buy the same models, the difference between firms is how they use them: what data the models may see, how output is checked, what is recorded, and who answers for it. Clients, regulators and insurers are all starting to ask those questions directly. The firms that can answer them with evidence rather than assurances will win the work that matters, and the professionals who thrive will be the ones who ask better questions, handle ambiguity, keep a client's trust and exercise judgment the machine cannot be held accountable for.
sections.heading: Governance becomes what firms compete on

sections.body: Each profession below has its own section, listed in alphabetical order: the accountant, the economist, the lawyer, the physician and the researcher. Each has ten areas and fifty topics, written the same way, from what the work is to what it runs on, how it is done, where the risk and the rights sit, and where it is going.
